summary: Cape Norman Light, at the northern tip of Newfoundland on the Strait of Belle Isle, was first lit in 1871; its concrete tower dates from 1964.

structures.type: white octagonal tower with red top

staffing.note: Keeper listed from 2002 to at least 2017 (LighthouseFriends). Automated 1992-2002.

access.note: Canadian Coast Guard station; keepers' home and workplace. Grounds open, tower closed.

events.note: Wooden hexagonal tower built 1870-71 (40 ft base to vane); station cost $10,141.96
Henry Locke appointed first keeper at $500 a year
Dominion Line steamer Montreal aground on Belle Isle in fog, 4 August 1889; not at Cape Norman
Steam fog alarm installed at Cape Norman after the Montreal loss; in operation a year after the wreck (LighthouseFriends)
Changed to triple flashing, because Cape Bauld became a double flash (Marine report for the year ending 1906)
Segmental cast-iron tower built to replace the 1871 wooden tower; in operation 1907 (LighthouseFriends)
New fog alarm building with a three-inch diaphone completed (LighthouseFriends)
Old wooden tower razed to first floor and converted into a storehouse
Fog alarm converted from steam to oil
Concrete tower completed (contract let 1963); still standing
Station automated; keeper's post empty for about ten years
Warren Campbell hired as keeper, as printed by LighthouseFriends

corrections.proposed: 1871 wooden tower (about 12 m) razed to first floor 1909 and no longer a standing tower; the 15.2 m tower on the List of Lights is the concrete tower built 1964
corrections.why: The record attaches the 15 m height to the 1871 tower. LighthouseFriends and the Marine reports describe the 1871 tower as wooden, 40 ft base to vane, and razed to its first floor in 1909. The Coast Guard list gives 15.2 m for the present tower.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikidata and Wikipedia give 35 m; the Coast Guard List of Lights gives 38.7 m for the present light. The current List figure is used. LighthouseFriends gives the 1871 focal plane as 138 ft (42 m) above sea level.

The List gives Fl(3) W 27s; Wikipedia gives Fl(3) W 30s. The 1906-07 triple-flash apparatus described by LighthouseFriends has a 30-second cycle, so the change from 30 to 27 seconds is not dated in the sources read.

notes_for_editor: Positions and roles: the keepers come from LighthouseFriends' roster and Marine keeper tables (matched by position in OCR column blocks for 1904 and 1906). John William Campbell (LighthouseFriends) is also called John Warren Campbell (Wikipedia); the Marine tables print 'Campbell, John W.'. Wikipedia says Campbell arrived at Cape Norman 'on board the SS Montreal' in July 1890. The Montreal was wrecked on Belle Isle in August 1889 (New-York Tribune), so that claim is not used. The 1871 construction details, the 1870 Department of Marine statement and John Page's 1860 letter are quoted by LighthouseFriends. The Canadian annual reports in the corpus begin in 1900, and the 1870-71 sources were not checked against a primary document. The fog-alarm link to the Montreal loss is LighthouseFriends' claim (Wikipedia gives the same link); no 1890 report was read. LighthouseFriends' claim that wreckers plundered the Montreal's cargo has no second source and is left out. Living or recent keepers: Alvin Campbell and Warren Campbell are named only as LighthouseFriends' roster prints them, with no personal details. Current staffing (2026) is not verified beyond the 2017 roster line. Record conflicts: focal height 35 m (Wikidata) against 38.7 m (List of Lights); characteristic 30 s (Wikidata/Wikipedia) against 27 s (List of Lights); the 1871 tower entry as standing at 15 m (see corrections). The record location (51.62825, -55.90586) agrees with OSM, Wikidata and LighthouseFriends to within about 20 m. The List of Lights position (51 38 04.0 N, 055 54 37.5 W) is about 0.7 km away, and the sources read do not explain the difference. The record's 'built 1964' (Rowlett) is consistent with LighthouseFriends. Not checked: the Directory of Federal Heritage Designations and Parks Canada for any heritage designation; Newfoundland newspapers (not in the Chronicling America set). The Montreal wreck is sourced only to the New-York Tribune, 9 August 1889, page 1 (OCR; the page reports the steamer 'ashore' and the sixty people on the island). Verification 2026-10-28: the 1904 and 1906 keeper tables were read from the OCR page text, where each Campbell row (name, station, appointment date) sits on one line, so the pairing does not depend on column blocks. The page image could not be viewed from this session (archive.org returned only a 180-pixel thumbnail for the scan page), so the table pairing still needs an image check. The 1923 steam-to-oil date comes from LighthouseFriends; the fiscal 1924 Marine report records the change without a month, so the two are consistent but the month is not known.
